extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, inventors, and practitioners concerned with specification sufficiency and infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether a patent specification adequately discloses the invention (enablement, scope, and addressed skilled class) and whether a defendant's product is identical to the patented invention for infringement purposes. Focuses on the standards of evidence and the class of persons to whom the specification is addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — full and fair disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification ought to contain a full description of the way in which it is to be done; it must fairly and fully and properly give to the public the information which the public are entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, the specification should tell the public, without having recourse to experiments, how to do the invention or at least what course their experiments ought to take. If the specification does not give such information so as to render experiments unnecessary, it is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: No undue experimentation required
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is insufficient if it requires the skilled person to sit down and invent or to carry out experiments to discover how to make the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether an ordinary workman of competent skill could execute the invention from the specification and drawings using ordinary knowledge and mechanical means; if the worker must 'tax his invention' or perform trial-and-error to find the method, the specification is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled person standard (class of addressees)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of a specification is to be judged by the ability of the class of persons to whom the specification is presumed to be addressed (persons skilled in the art) to practise the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which class is applicable depends on the nature and objects of the invention: machines are often addressed to competent engineers or workmen in that trade; chemical compositions to practical chemists; novel inventions addressed to those with scientific knowledge. The specification is to be presumed addressed to those who would practically undertake to carry it out after the patent expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must not require more than ordinary trade knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not, in framing his specification, call upon the addressees to exercise more than the actual existing knowledge common to their trade or profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee may exhaust the common knowledge of the trade but cannot require the exercise of inventive faculty by the intended workmen. If application of the directions requires solving a new problem or exercising invention beyond ordinary skill, the specification is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and weight of practical (artisan) evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence from persons practically engaged in the relevant trade (artisans/workmen) is important to show whether the specification enables practical making, constructing, compounding, and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mere artisan can, from the specification, make or construct the thing, that is cogent evidence of sufficiency. The artisan's testimony is particularly appropriate to show practical sufficiency where a class of such workmen would be expected to practise the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of scientific testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific witnesses (persons thoroughly conversant with the science underlying the invention) may demonstrate or teach an artisan how to apply the specification, but their evidence cannot substitute for a specification that leaves an artisan unable to practise the invention unaided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such witnesses can show that a means would succeed, the law generally does not permit curing an obscure specification exclusively by the fresh invention or correction of a scientific person; ordinary workmen's ability remains the primary standard unless the invention is inherently scientific.

rubrics_metrics.name: When specification is addressed to engineers/scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is of a character addressed to scientific witnesses (not within province of ordinary artisans), the specification may be presumed addressed to men capable of applying the scientific principles and should furnish rules by which such persons can determine required parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for an invention requiring selecting a particular angle for paddle entry, the specification should furnish the rules and mechanical means for engineers to ascertain and apply that angle; the expected skill level of addressees rises with the invention's scientific character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of drawings — illustrative not limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing in a specification is generally to be treated as illustrative of the invention and not as confining the invention to the particular angle, position, or dimension shown unless the specification so confines it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should look to the substance of the disclosure rather than literal conformity to a drawing. Discard exaggerated or impossible cases drawn and focus on whether the specification supplies directions for ordinary cases likely to occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose practical adjustments/details
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should state practical adjustments or details necessary for the invention to work in practice (e.g., making rods of different lengths), or, if they cannot be fully ascertained, it should so state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of such practical details that would force a workman to experiment (and prevent them from discerning necessary modifications) renders the specification insufficient. If a small adjustment is necessary (like tallow or differing rod lengths), it should be mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: No retention of secret after patent term (duty to teach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees are bound to set out fully and fairly what their invention is so the public can carry it into effect after the patent term; they must not keep essential secrets such that the public cannot use the invention when the patent expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy: it would be a hardship if a patentee obtained exclusive rights but failed to teach how to operate the invention, thereby keeping the public from practising it after expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discard unrealistic/extreme embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing sufficiency, exaggerated or impossible cases (e.g., angles that cause parts to go beyond physical limits) should be discarded; assessment should focus on ordinary practicable cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the substance and to whether the information communicated would be enough in ordinary cases likely to occur; one should not allow extreme hypothetical embodiments to defeat sufficiency where they are not practically required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical test phrasing — make/construct/compound/use
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should be expressed in such full, clear, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to make, construct, compound, and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classical statutory/judge-made test: proof that persons of ordinary skill can actually perform these acts from the disclosure is the decisive evidence of sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — identity with the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: On infringement, the question is whether the thing made or used by the defendant is, in the sense of the patent law, identical with the invention of the patentee; this is akin to the novelty/identity inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles of evidence applicable to determining whether two things are identical (as for novelty) apply to infringement. Analyze whether defendant's thing embodies the same invention as claimed.
